The Occupy Wall Street movement, which began two months ago, continues to gain momentum and attention across the United States. In Philadelphia, members of Occupy Philadelphia remained on site at City Hall into the evening of November 28, despite a deadline set by Mayor Nutter for them to leave. The protesters, who had set up a camp on the plaza, were served squash soup and water, and chanted slogans such as "What does democracy look like? This is what democracy looks like." Police looked on calmly, with Chief Inspector Joseph Sullivan stating that the police had no plans to evict anyone and that confrontation was not good.

In Los Angeles, the LAPD declared an unlawful assembly on the streets surrounding City Hall and ordered Occupy L.A. protesters to immediately disperse or face arrest. However, police stopped short of clearing the encampment, and four demonstrators were arrested during a brief confrontation. The Los Angeles encampment, which had grown to 400 tents and 700-800 people, was one of the largest on the West Coast. Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa had given protesters until midnight to remove their tents and leave, but police commanders later said they would permit the encampment to stay until at least daybreak.

In other cities, the Occupy movement continued to gain attention and support. In Oakland, police had used force against Occupy protesters, but in Los Angeles, police showed restraint, with one protester crediting them with being "fantastic." The movement, which is protesting economic inequality and excesses of the financial system, has gained support from organized labor, clergy, and civil rights groups.

The Occupy movement has also gained attention from high-profile figures, including hip-hop mogul Russell Simmons, who tweeted a message of support to Mayor Nutter, urging him to show restraint. The movement has also gained attention from the media, with many outlets covering the protests and the police response.

Overall, the Occupy movement continues to be a major story across the country, with protests and demonstrations taking place in cities from coast to coast. The movement's message of economic justice and restoration of balance to American society is resonating with many, and it remains to be seen how the movement will continue to evolve and grow in the coming weeks and months.

**Mikhail Kalashnikov's Legacy: A Life of Guilt and Redemption**

Mikhail Kalashnikov, the inventor of the iconic AK-47 assault rifle, passed away in December at the age of 94, leaving behind a complex legacy. In a surprising revelation, it has been reported that Kalashnikov wrote a lengthy emotional letter to the head of the Russian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Kirill, expressing his deep-seated guilt over the countless lives lost due to his invention.

The letter, written in May 2012, reveals Kalashnikov's spiritual pain and his struggle to come to terms with the devastating impact of his creation. He questioned whether he was responsible for the deaths of those who used his rifle, and wondered why God allowed humans to have "devilish desires" such as envy, greed, and aggression.

Kalashnikov's letter is a stark contrast to his earlier stance, where he refused to accept responsibility for the lives lost due to his rifle. He had previously blamed the policies of other countries that acquired the AK-47 for its misuse. However, in his later years, Kalashnikov seemed to have undergone a change of heart, seeking solace in the Russian Orthodox Church.

The inventor's journey to faith began at the age of 91, when he first entered a church. He was later baptized, and his letter to Patriarch Kirill reflects his newfound spirituality. The Patriarch's press secretary, Alexander Volkov, confirmed that the Church leader received Kalashnikov's letter and wrote a personal reply, stating that the Church supports those who create weapons to protect their country, but not those who use them for terrorist purposes.

Kalashnikov's legacy is a complex one, marked by both pride and guilt. His invention, the AK-47, has become a symbol of armed insurgent movements and has been used by child soldiers. However, it has also been a reliable and effective tool for defending one's country, as Kalashnikov intended.

As the world reflects on Kalashnikov's life and legacy, it is clear that his story is one of redemption and spiritual growth. Despite his guilt and pain, Kalashnikov found solace in his faith, and his letter to Patriarch Kirill serves as a testament to the power of human spirit and the search for meaning in life.

It contains this line: "I keep having the same unsolved question: if my rifle took away people's lives, then can it be that I ... am guilty for people's deaths, even if they were enemies?" On November 1, 2013, a gunman opened fire at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), killing one Transportation Security Administration (TSA) officer and wounding three others. The suspect, 23-year-old Paul Ciancia, was shot by airport police officers four times and taken into custody. He remains in fair condition at Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center.

The investigation into the shooting has raised questions about the response of police and fire officials. According to law enforcement officials, paramedics waited 150 yards away from the injured TSA officer, Gerardo Hernandez, because police had not declared the terminal safe to enter. Hernandez, 39, was shot in the chest and died at Harbor-UCLA Medical Center despite efforts to revive him.

An investigation is underway to determine whether a lack of coordination between police and fire officials prevented speedy treatment for Hernandez and other victims. TSA workers at LAX have expressed concerns about the lack of coordination between entities at the airport, which may have contributed to the delay in medical attention.

Ciancia, who is charged with killing Hernandez and wounding three others, including two other TSA officers, has been upgraded from critical to fair condition. He faces potential death sentence if convicted.

The incident has sparked a review of emergency response procedures at LAX and across the country. Los Angeles Police Department officials have acknowledged that they need to improve their response to active shooter situations, and a recent audit found that only 250 sworn officers in the Metropolitan Division had received refresher training in first aid and CPR.

A public memorial service was held on Tuesday to honor Gerardo Hernandez, the first TSA officer killed in the line of duty. The incident has raised concerns about the safety of airport employees and the need for improved emergency response procedures.

Officers checked on Hernandez, who was just 20 feet from an exit, then moved on while paramedics waited 150 yards away, the AP reports, noting it's not clear if immediate attention might have saved Hernandez's life. Now under review: the conversations took place between police and fire commanders to determine when it was safe enough to enter, and whether paramedics could have gone into the terminal earlier. While an officer who checked on Hernandez about 5 minutes after he was shot told numerous officers he was dead, the AP reports that it's not known whether that officer had the training needed to make that determination; no first-aid was administered. "I basically think there's a lack of coordination between entities at this airport. That lack of coordination may have led to something that shouldn't have happened," an LAX employee says. "We may be talking about Officer Hernandez as a survivor." The results of the investigation could be months away, the AP adds. Ciancia was on Tuesday upgraded from critical to fair condition at UCLA Medical Center.

The Muslim Brotherhood, from which Morsi hails, has demanded that any political solution be based on "the return of the president," referring to reinstating Morsi to power and restoring the country's Islamist-dominated parliament and constitution. Ashton's visit marked a significant effort by the EU to mediate a resolution to Egypt's crisis, and her meeting with Morsi was seen as a crucial step towards finding a way forward. **Oldest Cold Case Ever Brought to Court: Man Freed After 58 Years**

In a stunning turn of events, Jack McCullough, 76, has been released from prison after serving a life sentence for the 1957 murder of 7-year-old Maria Ridulph. A judge, William Brady, ordered McCullough's release and granted him a new trial, citing "clear and convincing evidence" that he was wrongly convicted.

The case, which went cold for half a century, was reopened in 2008 after a tip from McCullough's half-sister. McCullough was convicted in 2012 and sentenced to life in prison, but a new investigation by DeKalb County State's Attorney Richard Schmack found that the evidence used to convict him was flawed.

Schmack's review of the case, which included a review of 4,500 pages of documents, found that McCullough's alibi, which he had maintained for decades, was supported by newly discovered phone records. The records showed that McCullough had made a collect call to his parents at 6:57 p.m. from a phone booth in downtown Rockford, which is 40 miles northwest of where Maria was abducted.

The prosecution's case against McCullough was based on the testimony of Maria's friend, Kathy Sigman, who identified McCullough as the killer from an array of six photographs. However, Schmack noted that the photographs were not taken at the same time, and McCullough's picture stood out because everyone else wore suitcoats and had professional yearbook pictures.

Maria's family remains convinced that McCullough is guilty and has sought the appointment of a special prosecutor to keep him behind bars. However, the judge's ruling has brought a sense of closure to McCullough, who was seen smiling and hugging his family members after the hearing.

The case has raised questions about the reliability of eyewitness testimony and the importance of thorough investigations in cold cases. It is a rare example of a wrongful conviction being overturned, and it highlights the need for prosecutors to re-examine evidence and consider new evidence in cases where doubts have been raised.

McCullough's release has been hailed as a victory for justice, and it brings an end to a 58-year-old case that has haunted the community of Sycamore, Illinois.
details.ground_truth: A man convicted four years ago in the oldest cold case ever tried was freed Friday after an Illinois judge vacated his conviction and subsequent life sentence, CNN reports. According to CBS News, 76-year-old Jack McCullough was convicted of kidnapping a 7-year-old girl, choking her, and stabbing her to death in 1957. The case was reopened in 2008, and McCullough was arrested in 2011 and convicted the following year. After an appeal by McCullough, Illinois state's attorney Richard Schmack launched a six-month investigation that found what he calls "clear and convincing evidence" that McCullough is innocent. While the judge Friday vacated McCullough's conviction, he stopped short of declaring him innocent, and a new trial will be held, the Chicago Tribune reports. McCullough, who lived in the same neighborhood as the kidnapped girl, says he was 40 miles away at an Air Force recruiting center at the time of the kidnapping. It's an alibi that passed a polygraph test in 1957 and made it impossible for him to be the culprit based on the FBI's original timeline for the kidnapping. That timeline was later changed by police, and Schmack says documents—including phone and Air Force records—supporting McCullough's alibi were wrongly not allowed at his trial. A friend of the kidnapped girl picked McCullough out of a photo lineup when the case was reopened. But his was the only non-yearbook photo in the lineup, and she picked a different man out of a photo lineup 50 years earlier. That info wasn't allowed at McCullough's trial either. No physical evidence was ever found to support McCullough's conviction.

**Cigarette Smoke Fuels the Rise of Superbugs: A Growing Concern**

Recent research has shed light on the alarming effects of cigarette smoke on the virulent rampage of superbugs, specifically Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Studies conducted by researchers at the University of California, San Diego School of Medicine have found that cigarette smoke not only harms human respiratory and immune cells but also makes MRSA more resistant to antibiotics and immune responses.

According to the studies, MRSA exposed to cigarette smoke extract becomes harder to kill, with macrophages (immune cells) struggling to eliminate the bacteria. The smoke-exposed MRSA was found to be more resistant to reactive oxygen species and antimicrobial peptides, which are essential for killing pathogens. Furthermore, the bacteria were able to adhere better to human cells, making it easier for them to invade and cause infections.

The research suggests that cigarette smoke alters the cell walls of MRSA, allowing it to repel common forms of immune responses. This effect is dose-dependent, with higher levels of smoke extract leading to increased resistance. The study also found that the increased resistance continued for 24 hours after exposure, suggesting that it could be inherited.

In lab studies, MRSA exposed to cigarette smoke extract was found to be four times more resistant to macrophage killing than non-exposed MRSA. The smoke-exposed MRSA also became more aggressive, with a significant increase in mortality rates in mice. In contrast, e-cigarette vapor was found to have a lesser effect on MRSA resistance.

The findings of these studies have significant implications for public health, highlighting the need to avoid cigarette smoke to prevent the spread of superbugs. The research also suggests that cigarette smoke may be an additional contributing factor to the increased susceptibility of smokers to infectious diseases.

**Key Takeaways:**

* Cigarette smoke makes MRSA more resistant to antibiotics and immune responses.
* MRSA exposed to cigarette smoke extract becomes harder to kill, with macrophages struggling to eliminate the bacteria.
* The smoke-exposed MRSA is more resistant to reactive oxygen species and antimicrobial peptides.
* The bacteria are able to adhere better to human cells, making it easier for them to invade and cause infections.
* The increased resistance continues for 24 hours after exposure, suggesting that it could be inherited.
* Cigarette smoke is a significant contributor to the spread of superbugs, highlighting the need to avoid cigarette smoke to prevent the spread of infectious diseases.
details.ground_truth: Superbugs such as MRSA are already bad enough. But it turns out that something can make them even nastier: cigarette smoke. Researchers found that antibiotic-resistant bacteria exposed to the smoke became more aggressive and far more difficult to kill, they explain at Eureka Alert. It's almost as if the smoke sets off an alarm that causes the bacteria to strengthen its defenses, explains the Union-Tribune of San Diego. Scientists made the discovery by exposing immune cells to two different batches of MRSA, one normal and one treated with cigarette smoke extract. The bigger the dose of smoke, the bigger the effect, notes Medical Daily. "We already know that smoking cigarettes harms human respiratory and immune cells, and now we've shown that, on the flipside, smoke can also stress out invasive bacteria and make them more aggressive," says lead author Laura Crotty Alexander of UC San Diego. It's a double-whammy: Smokers already have weakened immune systems that make them more susceptible to infectious diseases, and the smoke they inhale seems to make invading pathogens even more dangerous. In this study, the smoke helped MRSA survive longer and kill more mice with pneumonia. (The latest antibiotic-resistant bug to make headlines is a nasty stomach virus.)

**The Most Influential People in the World: A Study of Wikipedia**

A recent study by the University of Toulouse's Young-Ho Eom has shed light on the most influential people in the world, based on their presence on Wikipedia. The study used a combination of algorithms, including PageRank and CheiRank, to analyze the links between Wikipedia articles and determine which individuals have the most important articles linking to them.

The initial results were surprising, with Frank Sinatra topping the list as the most important person in the English-language world, followed by Michael Jackson and Pope Pius XII. However, when the study was expanded to include all 24 major language editions of Wikipedia, the results changed. Adolf Hitler emerged as the most important historical figure, followed by Madonna and Michael Jackson.

However, the study's authors noted that these results were skewed by the presence of scientific names on Wikipedia, which led to Carl Linnaeus, the 18th-century Swedish naturalist, being ranked as the most important person in the world. Linnaeus' system of classification, which is still widely used today, resulted in a large number of links to his name, making him the most influential thinker in the world.

This finding was confirmed by a separate study, which used a different approach to calculate the influence of historical figures. The study, led by Jasleen Kaur and Filippo Radicchi, found that Karl Marx was the most influential scholar of all time, based on the frequency with which other academics referenced his work.

The Internet Archive, a non-profit organization, is also working to preserve the web by archiving pages and the links they contain. Their "No More 404" project aims to fix broken links on the web by preserving the original versions of pages and replacing links to them.

Overall, these studies highlight the importance of understanding the complex web of influences that shape our world. By analyzing the links between Wikipedia articles, researchers can gain insights into the most influential people and ideas in history.

Second place goes to Michael Jackson, and third to Pope Pius XII. When factoring in all 24 language editions of the online encyclopedia, the team found that Adolf Hitler ranked the most important person, while Michael Jackson was again second and Madonna third, reports the Guardian. "Our analysis shows that most important historical figures across Wikipedia language editions are born in western countries after the 17th century, and are male," the authors write. The researchers combined two algorithms to reach these conclusions. First, Google's PageRank algorithm, which determines a page's importance based on how many other pages link to it. In using PageRank on Wikipedia, the most important person in the world was 18th-century Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus, likely because the pages of organism after organism link back to the "father of taxonomy." So the researchers added an algorithm called CheiRank, which determines importance based on the number of outgoing links, the thought being that an important person would himself be connected to other important people, things, and events. Using the two together—an approach they dubbed 2DRank—no one beat out Frank Sinatra on English pages or Adolf Hitler across all language versions. **The Shroud of Turin: A Forensic Investigation Raises Questions about its Authenticity**

The Shroud of Turin, a 14-foot-long linen cloth bearing the image of a crucified man, has been a subject of debate and study for centuries. Recently, a team of forensic scientists conducted a thorough analysis of the bloodstain patterns on the shroud, which has led to some surprising conclusions.

According to the researchers, the bloodstain patterns on the shroud are inconsistent with the idea that it is a genuine death shroud of Jesus Christ. The team, led by forensic scientist Matteo Borrini and organic chemist Luigi Garlaschelli, used a technique called Bloodstain Pattern Analysis to study the flow of blood on the shroud. They created a mock-up of the shroud using a mannequin and synthetic blood, and then compared the results to the actual shroud.

The analysis revealed that the bloodstains on the shroud are inconsistent with each other, suggesting that a standing model was used to imprint the patterns at different angles. The researchers found that the bloodstains on the forearm and hand corresponded to an arm held straight out at 90 degrees to the side, while the hand marks matched an arm held out at 45 degrees. Some hand bloodstains even traced angles at odds with each other, off by as much as 10 degrees.

The team also found that the simulated spear wound in the chest ran in completely different patterns than the one on the shroud, whether the subject was standing or prone. Borrini stated, "This is just not what happens to a person on a cross." The researchers concluded that the bloodstain patterns on the shroud are more consistent with a medieval forgery than a genuine death shroud.

The Vatican has long regarded the Shroud of Turin as an icon, rather than a genuine religious relic, and has never officially weighed in on its authenticity. The radiocarbon dating of the shroud has determined its origin to be between 1260 and 1390, which further supports the idea that it is a medieval forgery.

While the findings of the forensic investigation are significant, they are not definitive. The researchers acknowledge that there may be other explanations for the bloodstain patterns on the shroud, and that further study is needed to fully understand the origins of this enigmatic artifact. Nevertheless, the results of this investigation have raised important questions about the authenticity of the Shroud of Turin and its place in history.

Researchers looking at the blood spatter found that the stains appeared to come from someone standing up, rather than someone who was flat on the fabric, Science Alert reports. As the researchers put it, the stains are "totally unrealistic" when compared to what they should look like. The shroud, which is held in the Cathedral of St. John the Baptist in Italy, is considered an icon, as opposed to a genuine religious relic, by the Vatican; Fox News notes "the church has never weighed in on its authenticity." "This is the kind of forensic work done all the time in police investigations," the forensic scientist who conducted the analysis tells BuzzFeed News. "Even a crucified or hanging person should leave a distinct blood pattern on the cloth, which would be fascinating information to have." The study found inconsistent staining, with researchers concluding multiple poses were used to create the bloodstains—a standing model was likely used to imprint patterns on the cloth at various angles for various body parts. President Barack Obama has signed a bill authorizing the Congressional Gold Medal, one of the highest civilian honors in the United States, to be awarded to over 6,000 Japanese-American veterans who served in World War II. These veterans, known as Nisei, were born to immigrant parents and were forced to fight for their country while their families were locked in detention camps due to their ethnicity.

The Congressional Gold Medal will be awarded to the 100th Infantry Battalion, the 442nd Regimental Combat Team, and the Military Intelligence Service for their heroic service and sacrifice during World War II. The 442nd Regimental Combat Team, made up of Americans of Japanese ancestry who volunteered to fight, is the most decorated Army unit of its size and length of service in the history of the United States.

The Nisei veterans, who were subjected to discriminatory treatment and labeled as "enemy aliens," proved their bravery and loyalty by serving in some of the most critical battles of the war. They played a crucial role in the rescue of the "Lost Battalion" in France and Italy, and their service paved the way for a more tolerant and just nation.

The Congressional Gold Medal is a testament to the sacrifices and contributions of these Japanese-American veterans, who risked their lives to defend their country while facing prejudice and discrimination. The award is a historic moment, recognizing the bravery and heroism of these individuals who have been overlooked for too long.

The award will be presented to the surviving veterans, including those from the Northwest, who have been waiting for this recognition for decades. The Congressional Gold Medal is one of the three highest civilian honors in the United States, and past recipients include the Wright Brothers, Rosa Parks, Navajo Code Talkers, the Tuskegee Airmen, and the Dalai Lama.

Microsoft has officially announced the name of its highly anticipated motion-control system, previously known as Project Natal, as Kinect. * Whitewater rafting and a racing game

* A Yoga/Tai Chi game
* A Soccer game
* Joyride, a racing game where players can steer using their hands

* Kinect Adventures, a game that lets players go river rafting with multiple players
* Dance Central, a dance-em-up game made by MTV Games

Kinect is seen as Microsoft's answer to Nintendo's Wii, which popularized game play without the need for a controller. A growing movement is underway to end the practice of institutionalizing children worldwide, with a goal of eradicating it by 2050. The charity Lumos, founded by author JK Rowling, is at the forefront of this effort. According to Lumos, 8 million children are currently separated from their families and locked away in institutions, often in atrocious conditions.

The problem is not limited to poverty-stricken countries, as even well-resourced institutions can cause irreparable harm to children. Research has shown that institutionalization can lead to stunting, developmental delays, and psychological trauma, as well as increased risk of abuse, trafficking, and poverty.

However, there is hope. Lumos has achieved significant success in several countries, including Moldova, the Czech Republic, and Bulgaria, where the number of children in institutions has decreased by as much as 75% in some areas. The charity estimates that with investment in inclusive education and health, support for vulnerable families, and alternative care options, the practice of institutionalization can be eradicated globally.

International donors play a crucial role in this effort, and Lumos is calling on them to prioritize funding for family-based care and community development. Ending institutionalization not only has a moral imperative but also makes economic sense, as it is far more cost-effective to support a child in a family than in an institution.

To raise awareness and build momentum for this effort, JK Rowling has launched the social media campaign #Letstalklumos, which encourages people to share their stories and support the cause. With a critical mass of expertise and evidence on hand, the time is ripe to make a difference in the lives of millions of children worldwide.

**Key Statistics:**

* 8 million children are separated from their families and locked away in institutions worldwide
* 70% reduction in children in institutions in Moldova since Lumos began working there in 2007
* 75% fall in admissions to institutions in Lumos's demonstration area in the Czech Republic
* 54% reduction in children in institutions in Bulgaria since Lumos began working there
* Goal to eradicate institutionalization by 2050

**Archaeological Discoveries Unveil Secrets of Britain's Ancient Past**

Recent excavations in Wiltshire, England, have uncovered significant archaeological finds that shed new light on Britain's prehistoric past. Two major discoveries have been made at Marden Henge and Wilsford Henge, both located in the Vale of Pewsey, a region known for its rich archaeological heritage.

At Marden Henge, a 4,300-year-old house, believed to be one of the best-preserved from the Neolithic period, has been unearthed. The house, which was likely used for ceremonial purposes, features beautifully worked flint arrowheads, decorated pottery, and a Roman brooch. Analysis of the site suggests that it was used for great gatherings, with pig bones and scorch marks indicating the presence of feasts. The house was abandoned, and the site was carefully covered with earth, suggesting that it was intentionally left untouched.

In a separate discovery, a 4,000-year-old Bronze Age skeleton, believed to be that of a child, has been found at Wilsford Henge. The skeleton, which is about 1.5m in length, was discovered wearing an amber necklace and lying in a foetal position. Scientific analysis of the skeleton is expected to provide valuable information on the child's diet, pathologies, and date of burial.

Both discoveries are part of a three-year excavation project, led by the University of Reading, in partnership with Historic England, the Arts and Humanities Research Council, and Wiltshire Museum. The project aims to gain a better understanding of the people who lived in the areas surrounding Stonehenge.

The excavations have also revealed the significance of Marden Henge, which is believed to be the largest prehistoric monument of its kind in the country. Built in 2,400 BC, the henge is larger than Avebury and 10 times the size of Stonehenge. The discovery of the house and the skeleton has shed new light on the purpose and significance of Marden Henge, which is thought to have been used for ceremonial and status purposes.

The findings from the excavations will be on display at an open day at Marden Henge, which will take place next weekend as part of the national festival of archaeology. The event will feature tours, activities, and displays of the finds, providing a unique opportunity for the public to learn about Britain's ancient past.

Archaeologists in Britain are excavating a monument ten times larger than the iconic structure, though it appears to the naked eye to be little more than farmland. A henge is a circular earthwork, and the one in question is Marden Henge, which sits a few miles north of Stonehenge in Wiltshire. National Geographic reports that roughly 4,500 years ago it featured 10-foot-tall earthen berms that encompassed some 40 acres. The Guardian writes that the henge was "far larger than the Avebury or Stonehenge circles, and too large for any imaginable practical use." But over the ages Marden Henge's berms have "slumped" and farmers have worked the land, and archaeologists have gravitated to the more breathtaking Stonehenge. Until now. Jim Leary of the University of Reading has just kicked off a three-year study of the site; his excavations (he worked at the site in 2010, too) are the only ones to have occurred there in nearly 50 years. He hopes the berms will help explain the "insane, utterly unsustainable" construction boom that led to Marden Henge and four other nearby Neolithic monuments, including Stonehenge. "Not nearly enough attention has been paid to the archaeology of the fertile valley in between these places," says Leary. So far he's found the remains of a 4,000-year-old teen wearing an amber necklace just outside Marden Henge, per the BBC; fancy arrowheads; and a stone building within the henge containing the bones of at least 13 pigs, suggesting a huge feast was held there. "For all the attention that has been lavished on Stonehenge over the years, we may well find out that Marden was where it was really at during the Neolithic," he says. (There's a giant "super henge" under Stonehenge.)

The Pacific Crest Trail (PCT) has seen a significant increase in hikers following the release of the movie "Wild," which tells the story of Cheryl Strayed's 1,100-mile hike along the trail. According to the Pacific Crest Trail Association (PCTA), the number of long-distance hiking permits issued has increased by 300% since the movie's release, with over 4,000 permits issued in 2016 alone. This surge in hikers has raised concerns about overcrowding and the impact on the trail and its environment.

**Overcrowding and Environmental Concerns**

The PCTA has implemented a permit system to manage the number of hikers and mitigate the impact on the trail. However, the current system, which allows for 50 permits per day, is being pushed to its limits, with many hikers reporting long wait times and crowded campsites. The desert environments along the trail are particularly vulnerable to damage, and the PCTA is working to prevent erosion and protect the fragile ecosystems.

**Financial Costs and Safety Concerns**

The increased number of hikers has also led to a rise in helicopter evacuations and searches, which can be costly and resource-intensive. In the first 50 miles of the trail, there have already been 20 rescues in 2016. The PCTA is working to educate hikers about the importance of safety and responsible hiking practices.

**Impact on the Hiker Community**

The surge in hikers has also had an impact on the hiker community, with some long-time hikers expressing concerns about the loss of the trail's wild and peaceful nature. Rusty, a 71-year-old hiker who has completed the trail multiple times, said, "Sometimes, I'd like to hike without seeing a line of ants all the way to Canada."

**Alternatives to Thru-Hiking**

For those who are inspired to hike the PCT but are not prepared for a long-distance thru-hike, the PCTA recommends exploring shorter sections of the trail or taking a guided hike. The PCTA has also launched a campaign, #responsiblywild, to promote safety and responsible hiking practices.

**Conclusion**

The Pacific Crest Trail is a unique and challenging experience that has inspired many hikers to take on the adventure. However, the surge in hikers following the release of "Wild" has raised concerns about overcrowding and the impact on the trail and its environment. The
details.ground_truth: Hikers on the Pacific Crest Trail can expect to encounter harsh-but-beautiful landscapes, extreme fatigue, and—these days, at least—traffic. "You can’t talk about the Pacific Crest Trail without mentioning the crowds," Pete Brook writes for Outside. He should know: Brook currently is trekking the 2,650-mile PCT, which runs from the Mexican border through California, Oregon, and Washington to the border with Canada. But don't take his word for it: The Pacific Crest Trail Association so far this year has issued more than 4,000 permits to people planning on tackling at least 500 miles of the trail. To put things in perspective: 300 people attempted to complete the entire PCT in 2006, according to the AP, with about 120 of those making it. In 2014, 1,000 people set off and about half completed the trail. More traffic means more stress on the land, more improperly disposed of poop, and more inexperienced hikers requiring rescue. So what's with the increase in traffic over the past few years? You can thank Cheryl Strayed and her enormously popular memoir-turned-major-motion-picture Wild. After the book came out in 2012, there was a small increase in interest in the trail, the PCTA's Jack Haskel told the AP in 2015. But after the movie, starring Reese Witherspoon, was released in 2014, interest in the PCT exploded. "Millions are hearing about it now and are being inspired," Haskel said. Strayed, more or less unprepared for the journey, hiked 1,100 miles of the trail as a form of therapy as she grappled with personal demons. "However for others that follow her strategy of deliberate ineptitude, things might not turn out so well," writes DontHikeLikeWild.org. "Our advice to would-be hikers: Grow a spine first. Then get out there and hike the PCT." (This female hiker is the "biggest badass you've never heard of.")

**Rainbow-Colored Dinosaur Discovered in China**

A team of scientists has announced the discovery of a new species of dinosaur, Caihong juji, which lived 161 million years ago in what is now northeastern China. The dinosaur, which means "rainbow with a big crest" in Mandarin, is a small, bird-like theropod with a distinctive crest on its head and iridescent feathers on its head, neck, and chest.

**Unique Feathers**

The discovery of Caihong juji has shed new light on the evolution of feathers in dinosaurs. The dinosaur's feathers are unlike any others found in fossils, with a unique combination of long, flat melanosomes that are organized into sheets. These melanosomes are similar to those found in the iridescent throat feathers of hummingbirds, which create a metallic sheen that changes color with the viewing angle. The team suspects that Caihong's feathers may have glimmered with a rainbow of colors.

**Social or Sexual Display**

The researchers believe that Caihong's flashy display may have been used for social or sexual purposes, similar to the displays of modern peacocks. The dinosaur's body is bird-like, with feathers that may have been used for flight, but it also has a crested head that more closely resembles that of a Velociraptor.

**Oldest Known Animal with Asymmetrical Feathers**

Caihong is now the oldest known animal to have asymmetrical feathers, a key adaptation for flight. The dinosaur's frond-like tail has asymmetrical feathers, with short, stiff leading edges that would have borne the aerodynamic load of flight. This is a significant discovery, as it suggests that the evolution of flight in birds may have been more complex than previously thought.

**Evolution of Iridescent Color**

The discovery of Caihong's iridescent feathers has also shed new light on the evolution of iridescent color in small raptor dinosaurs. The team has found evidence of two different ways of creating iridescent color in these dinosaurs, which may have evolved independently.

**Further Study Needed**

While the discovery of Caihong juji is a significant one, there is still much to be learned about this dinosaur. The researchers hope to study the fossil further and learn more about the functions of its iridescent feathers and asymmetrical tail.
details.ground_truth: Scientists are now saying there may have been "a more colorful Jurassic World than we previously imagined," thanks to the recent discovery of a fossil in China's Hebei province. Reuters reports that a closer look at the "exquisitely preserved," almost completely intact fossil of a crow-like dinosaur that lived about 161 million years ago revealed that Caihong juji had luminous, brilliantly hued feathers that closely resembled those of hummingbirds. The study in the journal Nature Communications documenting the find explains that "Caihong" means "rainbow" in Mandarin. Scientists think the colorful plumage, which appeared to have covered the bony-crested creature's head, neck, and chest areas, may have kept the dinosaur warm, as well as attracted potential mates; National Geographic compares it to peacock feathers. So how were researchers able to tell what color feathers the creature had from preserved bones? They used high-tech microscopes able to home in on 66 sites on the fossil, detecting tiny cell structures called melanosomes, which underlie pigmentation. Which colors they led to can be found by their shapes, and the melanosomes in Caihong were long and flat like pancakes—similar to those found in hummingbirds, which boast iridescent plumage. Although they can't pick out from the Pantone wheel Caihong's exact colors, researchers say the creature likely sported feathers with a "rainbow glimmer." Study co-author Xing Zu tells National Geographic that Caihong was a predator that spent its days gliding from tree to tree. And "glide" is the operative word, as this dinosaur likely didn't fly: Its feathers were located on its tail, not on its wings like birds, Discover notes. (A study postulated that nearly all dinosaurs had feathers.)

**Clarissa Dickson Wright: A Life of Passion, Food, and Controversy**

Clarissa Dickson Wright, the larger-than-life co-star and co-chef of the popular British television show "Two Fat Ladies," has passed away at the age of 66. Born on June 24, 1947, in London, Dickson Wright was a brilliant cook, food historian, and champion of hunting and shooting. She was known for her fiery temper, strong opinions, and unapologetic approach to life.

Dickson Wright's life was marked by both triumph and tragedy. She grew up in a wealthy family, but her father's abuse and alcoholism had a profound impact on her. She became a barrister at 21, but her drinking career soon took over, leading to a series of bankruptcies and a tumultuous personal life. However, after quitting drinking on her 40th birthday, Dickson Wright discovered a new passion for cooking and went on to become a celebrated food writer and television personality.

As one half of the "Two Fat Ladies" duo, Dickson Wright and her partner Jennifer Paterson traveled the UK in a motorcycle-sidecar, cooking up a storm and entertaining audiences with their irreverent humor and eccentricity. The show, which ran from 1996 to 1999, was a huge success and led to several books, including "Cooking With the Two Fat Ladies" and "A History of English Food."

After Paterson's death in 1999, Dickson Wright continued to work in television, fronting several shows, including "Breakfast, Lunch and Dinner" and "Clarissa and the Countryman." She was also a vocal advocate for rural life and hunting, causing controversy with her views on the badger cull and her suggestion that people should eat the meat of culled badgers.

Throughout her life, Dickson Wright was known for her intelligence, wit, and unapologetic approach to life. She was a true original, and her passing has left a void in the world of food and television. As her agent said, "Her fun and laughter, extraordinary learning and intelligence, will be missed always, by so many of us."
details.ground_truth: Both of TV's "Fat Ladies" have sung. Clarissa Dickson Wright, one half of the BBC's "Two Fat Ladies" cooking duo, died in Edinburgh Saturday at age 66, the BBC reports. Wright was a former lawyer who filmed four of the "Fat Ladies" series, going on food-related road trips across the UK in a motorbike and sidecar with Jennifer Paterson, before Paterson died in 1999 from cancer. The New York Times describes Wright as a "rebel," both hosts as "irreverent and eccentric," and the recipes as "sometimes confounding." Wright's eclectic working life also included stints as a cook, an author, and a cookbook shop manager; she also ran a catering business, was a guild butcher, and once worked on a yacht in the Caribbean. In fact, she recently said, "I've had a fantastic life and I've done everything I could have wanted to do and more." It wasn't until her 40s, after she'd recovered from alcoholism, that she got into cooking seriously. As for the perhaps-controversial title of the show that brought her fame? "If you're fat you're fat," she once said. "I hate this modern-day political correctness, that you don't call things by their proper name." Her agent remembers Wright similarly in a statement: "Loved dearly by her friends and many fans all over the world, Clarissa was utterly non-PC and fought for what she believed in, always, with no thought to her own personal cost." **Tragic Death of Experienced Mountain Walker**

A 53-year-old woman, Jane Wilson, fell to her death while attempting to navigate a mountain in Snowdonia, Wales. Wilson, an experienced mountain walker and librarian at the University of Manchester, was with her husband Gary on a walk on March 25. They had decided not to attempt to reach the summit of Tryfan, a notorious mountain known for its steep inclines and loose rocks.

Using only Gary's smartphone to guide them, they headed across the mountain's west face, a route that has been described as "not a straightforward path" by Chris Lloyd, a member of the Ogwen Valley Mountain Rescue Team. Wilson fell 20-30 feet down a vertical cliff and then tumbled 150 meters down into a rocky area known as Notch arrete. She suffered severe injuries, including a fractured skull, and was pronounced dead at the scene.

The inquest into Wilson's death heard that the couple had been using a smartphone app to navigate the mountain, rather than a traditional map and compass. The coroner, John Gittins, recorded a conclusion of accidental death.

Experts have warned that relying on smartphone apps to navigate mountains can be hazardous, particularly in areas with poor phone signal or limited battery life. Mountain Rescue England and Wales has urged walkers to use a map and compass in addition to electronic navigation aids.

The incident has highlighted the risks of mountain walking and the importance of proper planning and preparation. Tryfan is a particularly challenging mountain, with over 30% of incidents involving the Ogwen Valley Mountain Rescue Team occurring on this peak.

The coroner's conclusion of accidental death has been met with sadness and regret, as Wilson was a fit and active woman who had been mountain walking and scrambling for six years. Her death serves as a reminder of the importance of caution and respect for the natural environment when engaging in outdoor activities.
details.ground_truth: A hiker's fatal fall in March has been blamed on using a smartphone app map instead of an actual map. While attempting to descend the mountain, Gary was looking at an Ordnance Survey app while Jane went a short way ahead to make sure the path was safe, according to the Telegraph. The Manchester Evening News reports Gary heard his wife fall, got to safety, and called for help. Rescuers found the 53-year-old librarian's body at the bottom of a 30-foot cliff with a fractured skull. At a hearing Friday, Jane's was ruled an accidental death due, in part, to using an app instead of a map. "Apart from potential difficulties caused by poor detail on an electronic map, batteries on mobile phones have a nasty habit of running out just when you need them most," the Telegraph quotes a spokesperson for Mountain Rescue England and Wales as saying. A detective says the app map "would have been small and not as detailed" and took the couple on a route that was not the safest. A director with Ordnance Survey says hikers should always use the app in conjunction with an actual map "due to the nature of mobile devices when navigating the real world." Authorities also say Jane wasn't wearing appropriate footwear for the hike. (Go inside the futile search for "Inchworm" on the trail.)

The failures of these soda taxes have been attributed to several factors, including the regressive nature of the tax, which disproportionately affects low-income families. A former sales executive for Intermex Wire Transfer LLC, a money-transfer company, has filed a lawsuit against her former employer alleging that she was fired for refusing to install a location-tracking app on her company-issued iPhone. In recent weeks, two major retailers, Neiman Marcus and Target, have been hit by significant data breaches, compromising the sensitive information of millions of customers. Neiman Marcus has apologized for not disclosing the breach sooner, citing a need to confirm evidence before notifying customers. The company has offered one free year of credit monitoring to affected customers.

**Target Breach**

Target, which disclosed its breach on December 19, reported that 40 million credit- and debit-card accounts were compromised, along with encrypted PINs for debit cards. The breach was caused by a type of malware, similar to a computer virus, placed in a store's point-of-sale systems. The breaches have led to criticism of the retailers for not disclosing the incidents sooner, with some questioning the timing of Neiman Marcus's announcement on January 1, after the holiday season.

**Future Risks**

The report from iSight warns that the type of POS hacking used in the Target breach is "new to eCrime" and can net big rewards for cyber crooks with little risk. Astronomers and scientists are exploring the possibility of advanced civilizations harnessing energy from distant stars to sustain their growth and prevent being left behind in the vast expanse of space. details.ground_truth: For decades, the human story was one told through signs of modernity—art, tools, burials—found only after Homo sapiens left Africa. Recent discoveries pushing back the date of departure are helping to change that narrative, as are three new studies in Science. Together, they describe the earliest stone tools of their kind in East Africa as well as the earliest evidence for long-distance transport of raw materials in the region, per Science News. Researchers previously believed the Early Stone Age marked by large, primitive tools (hand axes and cleavers) made way for the Middle Stone Age and its smaller tools (spearpoints and blades) around 280,000 years ago. But stone tools found in Kenya's Olorgesailie Basin show hominin groups—it's not clear which species is responsible—had developed these more advanced tools approximately 320,000 years ago. "We see a smaller technology, a more diverse series of stone tools … designed for specific purposes," researcher Rick Potts tells NPR. An expert not involved in the study says the tools are so "prepared and retouched" they suggest the Middle Stone Age likely started even earlier. What drove it? Microscopic and chemical analyses of the region's soil show the landscape was rapidly shifting between wet and dry conditions, meaning hominins might have been forced to adapt. But as the technology also coincides with the emergence of Homo sapiens in Africa, it's possible that the human mind deserves credit. The tools themselves suggest the development of trading networks, too. Some were made of rocks carried from 55 miles away, says Potts. Others were made of obsidian from as far as 30 miles away, per the Conversation. (These stone tools are also making waves.)

**Search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 Continues with New Leads**

The search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370, which disappeared on March 8 with 239 people on board, has entered its most intensive phase as search teams investigate new leads in the southern Indian Ocean. A Chinese ship, Haixun 01, has picked up a pulse signal with a frequency of 37.5kHz, consistent with those emitted by the flight recorders. However, there is no confirmation yet that the signal is linked to MH370.

The signal was detected on Saturday at about 25 degrees south latitude and 101 degrees east longitude, and was heard by three people on board the ship. The Australian agency co-ordinating the search, led by Angus Houston, has confirmed that the reported signals "are consistent with the aircraft black box" but "there is no confirmation at this stage that the signals and the objects are related to the missing aircraft."

The search area, covering about 217,000 sq km (84,000 sq miles), has been narrowed down to a specific location based on analysis of satellite data. Two ships, Australian naval vessel Ocean Shield and HMS Echo, are using underwater locator capabilities to detect an underwater signal emitted by the data recorders. The battery-powered signal fades after 30 days, and Monday marks day 30 since the plane disappeared.

The search operation has been joined by dozens of ships and planes, including a British Royal Navy vessel, which is on its way to the area where the Chinese ship detected the signal. The Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA) has planned to search three separate areas on Sunday, with up to 10 military planes, two civil aircraft, and 13 ships assisting in the search.

While the new lead has raised hopes that the search may be nearing a breakthrough, experts caution that it is still too early to confirm whether the signal is linked to MH370. Oceanographer Simon Boxall noted that there have been many promising leads in the past that have turned out to be nothing, and that the search team needs to be cautious.

The investigation into the disappearance of MH370 continues, with Malaysia announcing the establishment of three ministerial committees to help co-ordinate the search and a new investigation team that will include members from Australia, China, the US, the UK, and France.
details.ground_truth: Could it be? A Chinese ship searching for Flight 370 has picked up a ping in the southern Indian Ocean, reports CNN and the BBC. All the reports caution that it could turn out to be yet another false hope, however. "This could be a variety of things," says one oceanographer, noting that the frequency is used by lots of instruments. For the record, the Chinese ship detected the signal at 25 degrees south latitude and 101 degrees east longitude, says the state-run Xinhua. "It is yet to be established whether it is related to the missing jet," the report says. The development comes as dozens of ships and planes intensify their sweeps in the search zone, given the finite battery life of the data recorders.

**Habeas Corpus: A Fundamental Right Under Threat**

Habeas corpus, a cornerstone of Western law, has been a vital safeguard against government overreach and abuse of power. This ancient legal procedure, enshrined in the US Constitution, ensures that individuals cannot be held indefinitely without cause. However, in recent years, the right to habeas corpus has been eroded, particularly in the context of the War on Terror.

**Guantanamo Bay and the Military Commissions Act**

The Military Commissions Act (MCA) of 2006 revoked the right to habeas corpus for detainees at Guantanamo Bay and for non-citizens labeled "enemy combatants" anywhere in the world. This provision applies to legal residents of the US, potentially leaving them vulnerable to indefinite detention without due process. The MCA has been criticized for its ill-considered and dangerous provisions, which undermine the fundamental right to habeas corpus.

**The Case of Guantanamo Detainees**

The majority of Guantanamo detainees were sold into captivity by warlords for bounties, with little or no evidence against them. Despite numerous legal victories affirming their right to challenge their detention, the Bush administration has prevented detainees from receiving a fair hearing in court. The Supreme Court has agreed to hear the detainees' cases for the third time, with the hope of upholding habeas corpus and holding the administration accountable.

**A New Frontier: Animal Rights and Habeas Corpus**

In a groundbreaking decision, a New York judge granted a pair of research chimpanzees, Hercules and Leo, the right to have their day in court through a writ of habeas corpus. This ruling marks the first time an animal has been covered by a writ of habeas corpus in US history, potentially paving the way for other animals to be recognized as legal persons. The Nonhuman Rights Project, which filed the case, aims to free chimpanzees and other cognitively complex animals from captivity and establish their right to bodily liberty.

**Implications and Future Directions**

The erosion of habeas corpus has far-reaching implications for human rights and the rule of law. If left unchecked, it could lead to a second-class system of justice, where certain individuals are denied due process and basic human rights. The case of the chimpanzees, Hercules and Leo, highlights the potential for habeas corpus to be used as a tool for animal rights and welfare. As the Nonhuman Rights Project continues to push for the recognition of animal personhood, the boundaries between human and animal rights may become increasingly blurred

NY Supreme Court Justice Barbara Jaffe ordered a university rep to address a suit filed by the Nonhuman Rights Project by appearing in court May 6 to argue why the college is holding Hercules and Leo. The group, which says the animals are being detained for biomedical experiments, says its ultimate goal is to have the animals released to the Save the Chimps sanctuary in Fort Pierce, Fla., per the NhRP's website. "This is a big step forward to getting what we are ultimately seeking: the right to bodily liberty for chimpanzees and other cognitively complex animals," Natalie Prosin, the project's executive director, tells Science. The case kicked off in December 2013 with lawsuits that also included two chimps held on private property; each case was struck down, sending the NhRP down the appeals path. Not everyone's convinced the upcoming hearing will mean liberation for the chimps. A Pepperdine University law professor tells Science that the judge likely just wants to hear both sides of the story: "It would be quite surprising if the judge intended to make a momentous substantive finding that chimpanzees are legal persons" without doing so, he notes. The Lacey Act, a century-old endangered species law, was amended in 2008 to include plants as well as animals. The law requires end users of endangered wood to certify the legality of their supply chain all the way to the trees. The Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA) has concluded that Gibson knowingly imported tainted wood, despite being aware of the risks involved.

Gibson denies the allegations, claiming that all of its purchases from Madagascar have complied with U.S. and Malagasy law. The company's CEO, Henry Juszkiewicz, has expressed frustration with the lack of clarity from the government on how the company has violated the law. The U.S. Justice Department has filed a court motion asserting that Gibson's Madagascar ebony was contraband, but has not commented further on the case.

The Lacey Act has also raised concerns among guitar builders and dealers, who worry about the retroactive nature of the law and the potential for forced compliance. Some have even warned clients to be wary of traveling abroad with old guitars, as the law requires owners to account for every wooden part of their instruments when re-entering the U.S.

In a separate development, the Internet Archive has been collecting and preserving web data through its Wayback Machine, which has been receiving daily data from Alexa Internet since 1996. This data is added to the archive after an embargo period, providing a valuable resource for researchers and historians.

* Gibson Guitar Corporation has been raided by federal marshals in Tennessee over allegations of trafficking in illegally obtained wood.
* The Lacey Act, a century-old endangered species law, requires end users of endangered wood to certify the legality of their supply chain.
* Gibson denies the allegations, claiming that all of its purchases from Madagascar have complied with U.S. and Malagasy law.
* The Lacey Act has raised concerns among guitar builders and dealers, who worry about the retroactive nature of the law and the potential for forced compliance.

On June 3, 21-year-old Rachel Borch was attacked by a rabid raccoon while jogging on a trail near her home in Hope, Maine. The raccoon, which was acting erratically and baring its teeth, charged at Borch, who was forced to defend herself with her bare hands. In a desperate bid to save herself, Borch drowned the raccoon in a puddle of water, holding its head underwater until it stopped struggling.

The raccoon was later confirmed to have tested positive for rabies by the Maine Center for Disease Control. Borch, who received six shots, including the rabies vaccine, immunoglobulin, and tetanus injections, is expected to receive her last injection this weekend. She has been taking antibiotics for the puncture wounds on her hands.

**Rabies Outbreak in Maine**

The incident is part of a larger outbreak of rabies in Maine, with 20 animals, including raccoons, red foxes, and skunks, testing positive for the disease as of June 7. In 2016, 64 animals in Maine tested positive for rabies, according to CDC data. The Maine CDC warns that if one animal tests positive for rabies, it's "almost 100 percent" certain there are other animals in the area also infected.

**Precautions and Prevention**

Maine animal control officer Heidi Blood advises residents to be cautious around wildlife, especially if they appear to be acting erratically or aggressively. Blood notes that an animal doesn't have to be aggressive to be infected, and that the rabies virus can live outside the body for 24 hours. Under Maine law, cats and dogs, even if they stay indoors, must be vaccinated against the disease.

**Warning to Residents**

The incident serves as a stark reminder of the dangers of rabies and the importance of taking precautions when interacting with wildlife. Residents are advised to be aware of their surroundings and to avoid approaching or touching animals that appear to be acting strangely.

If you visited the Red Planet roughly 4.3 billion years ago, that's what you likely would have found, say NASA scientists. Their new study arrived at that "solid estimate ... by determining how much water was lost to space," says lead author Geronimo Villanueva. While National Geographic observes the findings back up "reams of earlier evidence that water once existed on the surface" of Mars, another study author points out the assessment of the degree of water lost indicates something new. **University Professor Helps Rescue Student and Family from ISIS**

In a remarkable story of bravery and compassion, a Swedish university professor helped rescue her graduate student and his family from the clutches of ISIS in Iraq in 2014.

Charlotta Turner, a professor of Analytical Chemistry at Lund University, received a desperate text message from her student Firas Jumaah, who was hiding with his family in a disused bleach factory in Iraq. Jumaah, a member of the Yazidi minority, had fled to Iraq to be with his family after ISIS fighters took over their village, killing men and enslaving women.

Turner, who was shocked by the situation, contacted the university's security chief, Per Gustafson, who arranged for a rescue operation. A security company was hired, and a team of heavily-armed mercenaries was sent to Iraq to extract Jumaah and his family from the war zone.

The rescue operation was a success, and Jumaah and his family were safely evacuated to Erbil Airport, where they were reunited with Turner. Jumaah's family had been hiding in the northern mountains, preparing to flee to Syria, but Turner's intervention saved them from a potentially deadly situation.

The rescue operation was a unique event, and Gustafson said that it was the first time a university had been involved in such a mission. Jumaah, who had been working on his PhD at Lund University, was able to complete his studies and now works for a pharmaceuticals company in Malmö. His family has almost finished paying back the university for the rescue operation.

Turner's actions were motivated by her concern for her student's safety and her outrage at the actions of ISIS. "What was happening was completely unacceptable," she said. "I got so angry that IS was pushing itself into our world, exposing my doctoral student and his family to this, and disrupting the research."

The story of Turner's bravery and compassion has been widely reported, and it highlights the importance of academic institutions taking a stand against human rights abuses and supporting their students in times of crisis.

"I could hear that the situation was hopeless and they had to flee." The student, Firas Jumaah, was visiting his native Iraq to help family members during a brutal 2014 ISIS attack targeting Yazidis—a religious minority that includes his family. The terror group had just enslaved and massacred Yazidis by the thousand in nearby Sinjar. Now Jumaah and family were planning to flee to the mountains. "I had no hope at all," says Jumaah, per the Local. "I was desperate." But Turner took action. She spoke to Lund University's then-security chief, who contacted a company that sent mercenaries into northern Iraq. Only days later, four armed mercs on two Landcruisers blazed into the place where Jumaah was hiding, and rushed him to Erbil Airport with his wife and two young kids. "I have never felt so privileged, so VIP," he says. "But at the same time I felt like a coward as I left my mother and sisters behind me." Seeing his colleagues back in Sweden, he was speechless: "I just cried," he says. Yet Jumaah finished his PhD and found work at a Malmo pharmaceuticals company, and his family survived. The bill: roughly 60,000 kroner ($6,613), which his family has nearly finished paying. “If they told me to pay 200,000 kronor, I would,” says Jumaah. (The UN is finding fresh ISIS horrors.)

**Rare Celestial Event: Super Blue Blood Moon Total Eclipse on January 31, 2018**

A rare and spectacular celestial event is set to occur on January 31, 2018, when a total lunar eclipse, also known as a Super Blue Blood Moon, will be visible from eastern Asia to western North America. This event is a combination of a blue moon, a supermoon, and a total lunar eclipse, making it a once-in-a-lifetime experience for skywatchers.

**What is a Blue Moon?**
A blue moon occurs when there are two full moons in a single month, which happens about once every 2.7 years. The second full moon in a month is called a blue moon.

**What is a Supermoon?**
A supermoon is a full moon that occurs when the moon is at its closest point to Earth, making it appear 14% bigger and 30% brighter than a regular full moon.

**What is a Total Lunar Eclipse?**
A total lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth passes between the sun and the moon, casting a shadow on the moon's surface. During this event, the moon will take on a reddish hue, earning it the nickname "blood moon."

**When and Where to See the Event**
The total lunar eclipse will begin at 11:48am UTC on January 31, 2018, and reach its maximum at 1:30pm UTC. The event will be visible from eastern Asia to western North America, with the best viewing times in eastern Asia, Indonesia, New Zealand, and Australia.

**How to Watch the Event**
The Virtual Telescope project will provide a livestream of the event from Australia, starting at 11:30am UTC. Viewers can also watch the event with the naked eye, without any special glasses.

**Tips for Photographing the Event**
NASA's senior photographer Bill Ingalls recommends using a DSLR camera with a daylight white balance to capture the event. He also suggests putting the moon in context with a local landmark to create an original shot.

**Rare Occurrence**
This event is a rare occurrence, with the next total lunar eclipse of a blue moon happening on December 31, 2028, and the next one after that on January 31, 2037. The last time a blue moon passed through the Earth's umbra was on March 31, 1866.

Get ready to witness a rare and spectacular celestial event on January 31, 2018!

When the moon is at or near the closest point to Earth in its orbit (aka, a supermoon), it appears 14% bigger and 30% brighter than full moons that occur at the farthest point in the moon's orbit, though the moon will lose brightness as it enters Earth's shadow, according to NASA. Because of the way Earth's atmosphere bends light, the eclipsed moon will take on a reddish hue, something often referred to as a blood moon, making this rare celestial event "a super blue blood moon eclipse," according to the Miami Herald. The council has been criticized for its handling of the transition process, and many within the protest movement believe that Mubarak and his sons were only arrested and put on trial under pressure from massive protests.

The outcome of the elections and the trial will have significant implications for Egypt's future, with the country facing a difficult period of adjustment as it transitions to a new government and economy. The Brotherhood's potential victory in the elections could lead to a more Islamist government, while a conviction of Mubarak could provide a sense of closure for the victims of the crackdown and their families.
details.ground_truth: The final round of voting began in Egypt today, and it looks like the Muslim Brotherhood could walk off with a controlling majority of seats in Parliament's lower house. The Muslim Brotherhood's Freedom and Justice Party, the country's mainstream Islamist party, had already won a high percentage of the seats awarded in the first and second rounds of voting. Two of the nine provinces voting today are Brotherhood strongholds, where some of the party's most well-known candidates are running, the New York Times reports. A plurality, not a majority, was originally predicted for the Freedom and Justice Party. A majority would allow the party to govern alone, but the Brotherhood has repeatedly said it plans to form a coalition government, and has aligned itself with more liberal parties rather than the ultraconservative Salafis, who are in second place with up to 25% of the seats so far. Also today, prosecutors began presenting their case against former Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, Bloomberg notes. His trial resumed last week after a two-month break; state TV today showed Mubarak being carried to and from the courtroom on a gurney. "He deserves an end of humiliation and indignity," said the chief prosecutor, according to the AP.

**LOCAL NEWS SUMMARY**

**CAR SUSPENDED FROM TELEPHONE POLE IN MENDON**

A bizarre incident occurred in Mendon on Wednesday evening when a car was suspended from a telephone guy wire after the driver reacted too quickly to a GPS unit's instructions. Nabila Altahan, the driver of a Toyota Corolla, was heading westbound on Route 4 when her GPS device suddenly directed her to turn around, as she had passed her intended destination. Altahan's quick reaction to the directions caused her to leave the road, and the car ended up suspended from the guy wire of a telephone pole across from Sugar & Spice Restaurant.

Fortunately, neither Altahan nor her passenger was injured in the incident. State Police and the Rutland City Fire Department responded to the scene, and a witness at the nearby miniature golf course reported seeing the driver jump out of the car as it was suspended from the pole.

This unusual incident serves as a reminder to drivers to exercise caution when following GPS directions, and to take a moment to consider the consequences of sudden actions on the road.
